End-to-End Dynamic Sparsity for Resource-Adaptive LLM Inference

Yuhang Chen Affiliation: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill Work done during an internship at Meta.    Jinhao Duan Affiliation: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill    Ruichen Zhang Affiliation: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill    Mingfu Liang Affiliation: Meta AI    Xiaohan Wei Affiliation: Meta AI    Yunchen Pu Affiliation: Meta AI    Fei Tian Affiliation: Meta AI    Chonglin Sun Affiliation: Meta AI    Parish Aggarwal Affiliation: Meta AI    Frank Shyu Affiliation: Meta AI    Luke Simon Affiliation: Meta AI    Sandeep Pandey Affiliation: Meta AI    Tianlong Chen Affiliation: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill Joint corresponding authors.    Xi Liu Affiliation: Meta AI Joint corresponding authors.
Abstract

Large Language Models (LLMs) inference is typically deployed under a static resource assumption, where models execute a fixed computational graph regardless of the runtime environment. However, real-world cloud infrastructure is inherently dynamic, characterized by fluctuating availability (e.g., spot instance preemption) and tiered Quality-of-Service requirements. In such volatile settings, static models are inflexible: they either crash under resource constraints or waste compute on redundant operations. To bridge this gap, we propose Learning to Allocate (L2A), an end-to-end framework for resource-adaptive inference. Unlike prior adaptive methods that condition only on input difficulty, we formulate inference as a constrained resource allocation problem that conditions on both the input and the runtime resource budget itself. We introduce lightweight, budget-conditioned and input-aware gating networks integrated into the LLM. These gates are trained via a unified objective that jointly optimizes task performance, logical consistency, and resource costs decoupled along three axes that match how real-world dynamics manifest in deployment: layer skipping for memory and depth pressure, head pruning for throughput contention, and reasoning-token reduction for latency tightening. Crucially, this allows the model to learn a budget-aware policy beyond input difficulty alone: it adaptively configurates its computational footprint with respect to real-time resource dynamics, maximizing reasoning depth for complex tasks when resources permit, while enforcing strict frugality when budgets tighten. A single L2A model traces the entire compute-accuracy Pareto frontier on Llama-3-8B and Qwen-3-4B: at up to 34% realized layer sparsity, it stays within 0.6% of the dense baseline on GSM8K, with the same gap holding zero-shot on out-of-distribution tasks, while every static or heuristic baseline requires a separately tuned model and still drops by 5-10% at comparable inference time.

1 Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as the cornerstone of modern artificial intelligence (Brown et al., 2020; Ouyang et al., 2022), demonstrating remarkable capabilities across a wide range of tasks (Dubey et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024a). However, the deployment of these models in real-world production environments faces a fundamental and increasingly critical challenge: the mismatch between static inference architectures and dynamic resource availability. Current state-of-the-art LLMs are designed as static computational graphs. They operate under a rigid one-size-fits-all paradigm, activating every layer and attention head for every query, regardless of whether the input is a trivial factual question or a complex multi-step reasoning problem. This design assumes a stable, dedicated resource environment, which contradicts the reality of modern cloud computing.

In the real world, LLM inference occurs in dynamic, multi-tenant cloud environments where resources are unpredictable and fluctuate continuously. Available GPU memory and utilization limits can drop dramatically due to competing workloads. This volatility exposes the fragility of static inference systems. When resources shrink, static models face a binary choice: crash due to Out-of-Memory (OOM) errors or stall with unacceptable latency. They lack the elasticity to degrade gracefully. This limitation is particularly acute in two high-value scenarios: ❶ Task Survival under Preemption (Lin et al., 2022), where models running on low-cost Spot Instances receive a sudden shutdown warning (e.g., 2 minutes remaining) and must race to complete the inference before resources vanish; and ❷ Quality of Service (QoS) Differentiation (Li and Kumar, 2022), where service providers need to dynamically allocate compute budgets to serve different user tiers (e.g., Premium vs. Free) with varying quality-latency trade-offs. The central thesis of our work is that current LLM systems lack the necessary elasticity to handle these scenarios, leading to brittle and unreliable service.

Existing solutions to this efficiency problem fall short of runtime adaptability. Static compression methods like pruning (Ma et al., 2023; Ashkboos et al., 2024) and distillation (Hsieh et al., 2023) produce permanently smaller models that cannot scale up for hard tasks (Men et al., 2024). Conversely, dynamic inference techniques, such as early-exit networks (Xin et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020a; Schuster et al., 2022a), often rely on hand-crafted heuristics (e.g., entropy thresholds) that are brittle and struggle to generalize across diverse domains (Elhoushi et al., 2024; Jazbec et al., 2024). A critical open question remains:

To bridge this gap, we propose a novel framework for runtime-adaptive inference that unifies dynamic resource allocation with parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Unlike prior methods that treat model compression and adaptation as separate stages, we formulate the problem as a joint optimization objective. We introduce lightweight, input-dependent gating networks into the Transformer architecture, which learn to predict the necessity of each computational block (layers and heads) from the hidden states in real-time. By integrating these gates with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and a unified loss function that explicitly balances task performance, logical consistency, and multidimensional resource costs, we enable the model to learn an optimal, dynamic inference policy end-to-end.

We validate our framework through extensive experiments on a diverse suite of benchmarks (Gao et al., 2024), including GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), OpenWebText, and HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021). Our results demonstrate that our input-dependent, learned policy achieves a superior performance-efficiency Pareto frontier compared to static or heuristic baselines. Crucially, we show that our method learns a generalizable perception of task difficulty: it automatically reduces computation for simple inputs while preserving full capacity for hard reasoning tasks, even on out-of-distribution domains like code generation.

In conclusion, our core contributions are: (i) We propose a unified optimization framework for dynamic gating networks to learn input-dependent resource allocation policies end-to-end; (ii) We demonstrate through extensive experiments that our method achieves superior elasticity and robustness, effectively handling both resource fluctuations and QoS differentiation requirements.

2 Related Works

Efficient and Adaptive LLM Inference. Recent work studies conditional computation for Transformer-based LLMs, allocating depth per token/input rather than always executing all layers. Early-exit and adaptive inference methods (Schuster et al., 2022b; Liu et al., 2020b; Xin et al., 2020) train intermediate predictions to approximate the final output, enabling faster decoding on easy inputs (Schuster et al., 2022a; Elhoushi et al., 2024; Jazbec et al., 2024). Complementary approaches learn to skip computation inside the backbone: Mixture-of-Depths routes a subset of tokens through each layer under a fixed token budget (Raposo et al., 2024a), while layer-skipping methods learn lightweight predictors for when layers or submodules can be omitted during inference (Zeng et al., 2023b; Fan et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2025b) (Zeng et al., 2023a; Raposo et al., 2024b; Tan et al., 2024; He et al., 2024; Alizadeh et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2026). SkipGPT further highlights that stable, token-aware dynamic pruning benefits from decoupled policies and staged optimization (Zhao et al., 2025).

Model Compression under Deployment Constraints. A parallel literature compresses LLMs statically for deployment by removing weights or structures (e.g., heads/layers), then fine-tuning to recover accuracy (Ma et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Men et al., 2024) (Yang et al., 2024b; Zhang et al., 2024). More recent structured approaches compress LLMs by deleting rows/columns in weight matrices or other architecture-aware transformations to preserve throughput on commodity hardware (Ashkboos et al., 2024). These static methods are simple to deploy but typically produce a single fixed point on the accuracy–cost curve; meeting diverse runtime budgets often requires multiple models or additional control logic. Our framework complements static compression by learning input-dependent allocation at inference time.

Training Learned Gates. Learning to skip components introduces a training–inference gap (soft gates vs. hard decisions) and risks gate collapse. Prior work mitigates these issues via self-distillation and step-wise distillation, encouraging sparse students to match dense teachers and improving robustness of adaptive computation (Hsieh et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2020b; Zhang et al., 2022). In budgeted or cascaded systems, distillation-like objectives are also used to preserve decision quality while reducing cost (Fanconi and van der Schaar, 2025).

3 Methodology

In this section, we present our framework for Runtime-Adaptive Inference, which transforms the static computation graph of Large Language Models (LLMs) into a dynamic, input-dependent structure. We formulate the problem as a joint optimization of parameter-efficient adaptation and dynamic resource allocation. By introducing lightweight gating networks and a unified objective function, we enable the model to learn an optimal policy for skipping layers and pruning attention heads on-the-fly, balancing task performance with computational efficiency.

3.1 Preliminaries and Notations

We denote the frozen base language model by fθf_{\theta} and the parameter-efficient adapted model by fθ+Δ​θf_{\theta+\Delta\theta}, where Δ​θ\Delta\theta corresponds to the LoRA parameters. Given a tokenized sequence xx, we denote the next-token distributions of the teacher (dense) and student (budgeted) models by Pt(⋅∣x<t;θ)P_{t}(\cdot\mid x_{<t};\theta) and Ps(⋅∣x<t;θ,Δθ,Φ)P_{s}(\cdot\mid x_{<t};\theta,\Delta\theta,\Phi), respectively.

We study budget-conditioned dynamic execution in a Transformer with LL layers and HH attention heads per layer. The input hidden state of layer ll is hl−1∈ℝdh_{l-1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. To capture runtime constraints, we introduce a scalar budget signal b∈[0,1]b\in[0,1] (larger means more compute allowed) and map it to an embedding vector e⁡(b)e(b).

Our policy consists of layer gates αl​(⋅)∈(0,1)\alpha_{l}(\cdot)\in(0,1), head gates βl,h​(⋅)∈(0,1)\beta_{l,h}(\cdot)\in(0,1), and a budget-conditioned segment-transition gate τt​(⋅)∈(0,1)\tau_{t}(\cdot)\in(0,1). We denote the expected compute by 𝒞⁡(b)\mathcal{C}(b) and a monotone target budget by ℬ⁡(b)\mathcal{B}(b). For training objectives, we use ℒce\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ce}} for next-token cross-entropy, ℒkd\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{kd}} for KL distillation, and ℒ⁡(b)\mathcal{L}(b) for the total budget-conditioned loss. We use 𝒮\mathcal{S} to denote a mini-batch of inputs.

To make the transition behavior explicit, we assume a structured generation format <think>⋯\cdots</think> <answer>⋯\cdots</answer>. During training, we insert these tags into the target sequences so the model learns the segmentation. At inference time, the transition gate can force emitting the boundary token sequence </think><answer> to stop generating further reasoning tokens and enter the answer segment, rather than prematurely ending the whole sequence.

3.2 Learnable Dynamic Allocation Mechanism

To achieve fine-grained control over computational resources, we introduce learnable gating modules into the pre-trained LLM backbone. Crucially, our gates are budget-conditioned: in addition to hidden states, they take an external budget signal bb that specifies the maximum allowed compute.

Budget signal. We represent deployment constraints with a scalar budget b∈[0,1]b\in[0,1] (larger means more compute allowed) and feed it to all gating networks through a learned embedding e⁡(b)e(b). During training, we sample b∼𝒟b\sim\mathcal{D} to expose the policy to diverse operating regimes (we later ablate different choices of 𝒟\mathcal{D}). At inference time, bb is obtained by calibrating real-time system signals (e.g., deadline, queue length, memory headroom) into the same normalized range.

Dynamic Layer Skipping. For a Transformer layer ll, we introduce a lightweight gating network ϕL(l)\phi_{L}^{(l)} that produces a budget-conditioned scalar αl∈(0,1)\alpha_{l}\in(0,1):

αl​(hl−1,b)=σ⁡(MLPϕL(l)​([hl−1;e⁡(b)])),\alpha_{l}(h_{l-1},b)=\sigma\big(\text{MLP}_{\phi_{L}}^{(l)}([h_{l-1};e(b)])\big), (1)

where σ\sigma is the sigmoid and [⋅;⋅][\cdot;\cdot] is concatenation. The layer’s forward pass becomes a soft-gated residual hl=hl−1+αl⋅ℱl​(hl−1)h_{l}=h_{l-1}+\alpha_{l}\cdot\mathcal{F}_{l}(h_{l-1}), with ℱl\mathcal{F}_{l} the standard self-attention++MLP sub-layer mapping. During training αl\alpha_{l} scales the residual update so gradients flow into ϕL\phi_{L}; we optionally anneal the gate temperature to push αl\alpha_{l} near-binary by end of training. At inference, a hard threshold (e.g., 0.50.5) binarizes αl\alpha_{l}, physically skipping ℱl\mathcal{F}_{l} when αl\alpha_{l} falls below it.

Dynamic Head Pruning. Head gates βl,h∈(0,1)\beta_{l,h}\in(0,1) for each head hh in layer ll are produced by a network ϕH(l,h)\phi_{H}^{(l,h)} of the same form as Eq. 1, conditioned on (hl−1,b)(h_{l-1},b). The MHA output becomes a β\beta-weighted concatenation MHA​(hl−1)=[βl,1​Head1,…,βl,H​HeadH]​WO\text{MHA}(h_{l-1})=[\beta_{l,1}\,\text{Head}_{1},\dots,\beta_{l,H}\,\text{Head}_{H}]\,W_{O}, suppressing less relevant heads based on input context and budget. The wall-clock benefit from head pruning is implementation-dependent; our reported speedups come primarily from layer skipping and reasoning-length reduction.

Dynamic Reasoning-to-Answer Transition. Long reasoning traces often dominate inference latency on complex tasks. We add a transition gate τt∈(0,1)\tau_{t}\in(0,1), produced by ϕT\phi_{T} from (ht,b)(h_{t},b) at each generation step (same form as Eq. 1). During training, τt\tau_{t} remains soft and contributes to a reasoning-length cost (below); at inference, when τt\tau_{t} exceeds a threshold, we force-emit the boundary tokens </think><answer> (Section 3.1), after which decoding continues in the answer segment.

3.3 Parameter-Efficient Adaptation

Directly skipping layers or heads in a pre-trained model can severely disrupt its internal representations. To mitigate this and enable the model to adapt to sparse execution paths, we employ Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). We freeze the original model parameters W0W_{0} and inject trainable low-rank matrices Δ​W=B​A\Delta W=BA into the linear layers (Query, Key, Value, Output, etc.). The effective weight becomes W=W0+Δ​WW=W_{0}+\Delta W. This ensures that the optimization process is parameter-efficient and does not catastrophic forget the pre-trained knowledge, while allowing the backbone to adjust to the dynamic gating behavior.

3.4 Unified Optimization Objective

We define a unified loss function that jointly optimizes the LoRA parameters (WP​E​F​TW_{PEFT}) and the gating network parameters (Φ={ϕL,ϕH,ϕT}\Phi=\{\phi_{L},\phi_{H},\phi_{T}\}). The objective balances three competing goals: maximizing task accuracy, preserving the original model’s behavior, and satisfying a runtime budget.

For each training instance, we sample a budget b∼𝒟b\sim\mathcal{D} and condition all gates on bb. We then optimize a budget-constrained objective by penalizing deviations between the expected compute 𝒞⁡(b)\mathcal{C}(b) and the target budget ℬ⁡(b)\mathcal{B}(b):

ℒ⁡(b)=ℒce+γ⋅ℒkd+λ⋅(𝒞⁡(b)−ℬ⁡(b))+λT⋅ℛtok\begin{split}\mathcal{L}(b)=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ce}}+\gamma\cdot\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{kd}}+\lambda\cdot\big(\mathcal{C}(b)-\mathcal{B}(b)\big)+\lambda_{T}\cdot\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{tok}}\end{split} (2)

where λ\lambda controls the strength of budget enforcement and can be interpreted as a Lagrange multiplier.

Competence preservation and distillation. ℒce=−∑tlogPs(yt∣x<t;θ,Δθ,Φ)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ce}}=-\sum_{t}\log P_{s}(y_{t}\mid x_{<t};\theta,\Delta\theta,\Phi) is the standard next-token cross-entropy and preserves generative capability under sparsity. ℒkd=∑tDK​L(Pt∥Ps)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{kd}}=\sum_{t}D_{KL}(P_{t}\,\|\,P_{s}) is the forward-KL distillation from the frozen dense teacher and prevents the student from drifting when computation is skipped under tight budgets.

Budgeted compute cost. We estimate the expected compute as 𝒞⁡(b)=ℛL​(b)+ℛH​(b)\mathcal{C}(b)=\mathcal{R}_{L}(b)+\mathcal{R}_{H}(b), with

ℛL​(b)=1|𝒮|​L​∑x∈𝒮∑l=1Lαl​(x,b)​Cl,ℛH​(b)=1|𝒮|​L​H​∑x∈𝒮∑l,hβl,h​(x,b)​Ch,\mathcal{R}_{L}(b)=\tfrac{1}{|\mathcal{S}|L}\!\!\sum_{x\in\mathcal{S}}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\alpha_{l}(x,b)\,C_{l},\quad\mathcal{R}_{H}(b)=\tfrac{1}{|\mathcal{S}|LH}\!\!\sum_{x\in\mathcal{S}}\sum_{l,h}\beta_{l,h}(x,b)\,C_{h}, (3)

where Cl,ChC_{l},C_{h} are normalized per-layer / per-head FLOPs or latency costs. The target ℬ⁡(b)\mathcal{B}(b) is a monotone function of bb so larger bb permits more compute.

Reasoning length cost. Rather than penalizing per-component activation, here we penalize the expected length of the <think> segment via ℛtok=1|𝒮|​∑x∑t=1T(1−τt​(x))\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{tok}}=\tfrac{1}{|\mathcal{S}|}\sum_{x}\sum_{t=1}^{T}(1-\tau_{t}(x)). Minimizing ℛtok\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{tok}} pushes τt→1\tau_{t}\to 1 at earlier decoding steps, shortening reasoning under tight budgets while ℒce\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ce}} keeps the final answer correct.

3.5 Training and Inference

The training process involves an end-to-end joint optimization on a mixed dataset containing both simple and complex samples. For each sample, we additionally draw a budget b∼𝒟b\sim\mathcal{D} and condition the gates on bb. The gradients from ℒ⁡(b)\mathcal{L}(b) update both the LoRA parameters (to adapt to sparse execution paths) and the gating parameters (to learn a budget-aware routing policy). Intuitively, the budget term encourages the model to reduce compute under tight bb, while ℒce\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ce}} and ℒkd\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{kd}} preserve quality.

At inference time, we compute the budget-conditioned gates and replace soft gating with hard decisions. For layers, we skip the layer entirely if αl≤τ\alpha_{l}\leq\tau, achieving real-world acceleration without any specialized hardware support.

3.6 Inference-Time Budget Calibration

At deployment, bb is produced by calibrating real-time system constraints into the normalized range [0,1][0,1] to match the training-time support of b∼𝒟b\sim\mathcal{D}. We map multiple signals to intermediate budgets and take a conservative aggregate b=min⁡{btime,bmem,bqueue}b=\min\{b_{\mathrm{time}},b_{\mathrm{mem}},b_{\mathrm{queue}}\}. Given a request-level deadline TslaT_{\mathrm{sla}} and an online estimate of the dense-model latency T^dense​(x)\widehat{T}_{\mathrm{dense}}(x), we set btime=clip⁡(Tsla/T^dense​(x),0,1)b_{\mathrm{time}}=\mathrm{clip}(T_{\mathrm{sla}}/\widehat{T}_{\mathrm{dense}}(x),0,1), so tighter deadlines yield smaller budgets. When running on spot instances with remaining time-to-interruption TspotT_{\mathrm{spot}}, we further set bspot=clip⁡(Tspot/T^dense​(x),0,1)b_{\mathrm{spot}}=\mathrm{clip}(T_{\mathrm{spot}}/\widehat{T}_{\mathrm{dense}}(x),0,1) and update btime←min⁡(btime,bspot)b_{\mathrm{time}}\leftarrow\min(b_{\mathrm{time}},b_{\mathrm{spot}}). Memory and queue budgets bmem,bqueueb_{\mathrm{mem}},b_{\mathrm{queue}} are optionally computed from KV-cache headroom and queue length / utilization, clipped to [0,1][0,1], and combined via the same minimum.

4 Experiments

We design our experiments to rigorously validate two central hypotheses: (1) Our unified optimization framework with dynamic gating, achieves a superior performance-efficiency trade-off compared to static or heuristic methods. (2) The learned gating policy captures input-dependent difficulty features that generalize across tasks, enabling robust adaptive inference even on out-of-distribution (OOD) data.

4.1 Experimental Setup

Base models. We evaluate on two representative open-source backbones, Llama-3-8B (Dubey et al., 2024) and Qwen-3-4B (Yang et al., 2024a), to test whether the proposed gating-and-adaptation framework transfers across model families.

Datasets and evaluation split. We benchmark both in-distribution (ID) performance and out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness.

  • ∙\bullet

    ID training/calibration domains: OpenWebText (Gokaslan and Cohen, 2019) (OWT; general language modeling) and GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) (math reasoning, metric: accuracy). We additionally report results on MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021) (knowledge/QA; metric: accuracy) and Alpaca-Eval (Li et al., 2023) (instruction following; metric: score).

  • ∙\bullet

    OOD domains (held out during training): HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021) (Python code generation; metric: Pass@1) and Big-Bench Hard (Suzgun et al., 2023) (BBH; symbolic reasoning; metric: accuracy).

Decoding and prompting. All methods share the same prompt template, max-generation length, and stopping criteria; structured-format runs adopt <think>⋯\cdots</think><answer>⋯\cdots</answer> uniformly to isolate dynamic allocation from prompt engineering.

Baselines. We compare against (i) Original, the full dense model; (ii) Uniform pruning, every kk-th layer skipped irrespective of input; (iii) Oracle static pruning, layers / heads removed via offline profiling on ID calibration data; (iv) AdaSkip (He et al., 2025), an entropy-based early-exit heuristic; and (v) FlexiDepth (Luo et al., 2025a), learned adaptors with an auxiliary skipping loss.

Metrics. Quality: GSM8K / MMLU / BBH accuracy, Alpaca-Eval score, HumanEval Pass@1, and OWT perplexity. Efficiency: average realized layer / head sparsity, peak GPU memory, and total inference time. Definitions of efficiency metrics are in Table 1.

Implementation details. LoRA is applied to all linear layers at rank r=16r{=}16; the gate networks are 2-layer MLPs; we use a temperature-annealing schedule for the continuous gate relaxation (Liu et al., 2023) and switch to hard gating at inference. For representative operating points (Tables 2–3), each baseline is tuned to the same efficiency regime as our method (matched average time / sparsity), and the evaluation pipeline (batching, decoding, hardware) is held identical across methods.

4.2 Main Results

We present the primary comparison of our method against all baselines in terms of the accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier. The results demonstrate that our method consistently achieves the higher accuracy for any given computational budget. Specifically, under dynamic resource constraint, our method maintains near-lossless performance on GSM8K, whereas static uniform pruning suffers catastrophic degradation. While Oracle Static Pruning performs well on simple texts (OWT), it fails to adapt to the reasoning demands of GSM8K. Similarly, while AdaSkip offers some dynamic benefits, its reliance on entropy as a proxy for difficulty proves less robust than our learned difficulty features. This validates the effectiveness of our unified formulation in finding the optimal dynamic compression strategy.

Baseline Comparison. Table 2 and Table 3 summarize representative operating points on Llama-3-8B and Qwen-3-4B. Across both backbones, static pruning methods achieve meaningful speedups but suffer larger performance drops, especially on reasoning-intensive and OOD tasks, because they apply a fixed architecture to all inputs. In contrast, adaptive baselines (AdaSkip/FlexiDepth) better preserve performance under similar compute, and our method further closes the gap to the dense model while maintaining comparable latency. As shown in Figure 3, the learned policy tracks the externally provided budget signal by adjusting both the realized allocation and the average layer retention, while maintaining stable optimization dynamics.

Fixed-Budget Evaluation. To distinguish static resource constraints from dynamic resource-adaptive inference, we additionally evaluate a FixedBudget baseline, where a single global sparsity level is enforced for all inputs (i.e., the model cannot allocate more compute to hard examples). Table 4 reports results on Llama-3-8B under two budgets.

As the fixed budget tightens (higher global sparsity), we observe a consistent degradation across both ID and OOD tasks, reflecting the fundamental limitation of static allocation: it must under-compute on hard samples to satisfy the same budget that is appropriate for easy samples. This motivates our dynamic policy, which can preserve capacity on logically demanding inputs while still saving compute on trivial ones.

4.3 Cross-Task Generalization and Robustness

This section addresses the critical question of whether the learned policy simply overfits to the training data or learns a generalizable perception of difficulty. We conduct a Super Matrix cross-evaluation experiment, where models trained on single domains are tested against unseen domains.

As shown in Figure 4, the policy converges without gate collapse under a fixed budget, and the mean layer gate stabilizes after the initial adaptation phase.

Table 5 reveals a stark asymmetric failure mode in baselines. Models fine-tuned exclusively on easy data (OWT) reach high realized sparsity (∼\sim55%) but collapse on code generation (HumanEval Pass@1 12.8%→6.5%12.8\%\to 6.5\%), reflecting over-pruning on out-of-distribution hard inputs. Models fine-tuned exclusively on hard data (GSM8K) preserve task quality but fail to save compute on easy or instruction-style inputs (Sparsity ∼\sim10%), acting essentially as dense models. By contrast, training across mixed sources lets the policy modulate its sparsity by input domain: it stays conservative on hard reasoning while applying higher sparsity (∼\sim30%) on simple instruction following (Alpaca-Eval). This supports our hypothesis that the gating networks learn input-difficulty features that transfer across domains rather than memorizing domain-specific patterns.

4.4 Mechanism Analysis

We provide quantitative diagnostics to interpret the decision-making process and training stability of the learned gating networks. In particular, Figure 3 shows how the realized allocation behavior (and the mean gate α\alpha) tracks a time-varying budget schedule during training, while Figure 4 reports stable convergence of task loss and non-collapsing gate behavior under a fixed-budget setting.

Figure 3 shows that the policy tracks the non-stationary budget schedule by co-varying its mean gate α\alpha, while still optimizing stably (loss decreases). Figure 4 shows similar stability under fixed budgets, where tighter budgets converge to lower average α\alpha (more skipping) than looser budgets.

4.5 Ablation Studies

We validate the necessity of each component in our framework as shown in Table 6. Removing distillation (γ=0\gamma=0) causes a catastrophic collapse in reasoning capabilities (GSM8K: 35.8%→14.4%35.8\%\to 14.4\%), confirming its critical role in preserving logical consistency under aggressive pruning. Disabling the resource penalty (λ=0\lambda=0) results in a dense model with zero acceleration, proving that sparsity is explicitly driven by our objective. Furthermore, relying solely on layer skipping (β≡1\beta\equiv 1) is suboptimal; to match the same latency, it forces excessive depth reduction (62.5%62.5\%), degrading accuracy compared to our strategy (47.1%/30.8%47.1\%/30.8\%), which achieves a superior Pareto trade-off by distributing sparsity across both depth and width.

4.6 Discussion and Limitations

Our results should be interpreted in light of several practical considerations. First, the wall-clock benefit from head pruning can be implementation-dependent, whereas layer skipping and reasoning-length control yield more consistent acceleration. Second, the budget calibration mechanism in Section 3.6 assumes access to a reasonable online latency/memory estimator; errors in these estimates can lead to conservative or aggressive budgeting. Finally, the structured <think>/<answer> format provides explicit control over reasoning length, but requires consistent prompting and may not be equally applicable to all deployment settings.

5 Conclusion

We introduced L2A, a budget-conditioned framework that equips large language models with lightweight gating networks to dynamically allocate computation under runtime constraints. By jointly optimizing task loss, distillation, and budget-matching objectives, our approach can skip layers, suppress attention heads, and shorten the thinking segment while preserving the final answer quality. Experiments across multiple backbones and benchmarks demonstrate improved performance and efficiency trade-offs and stronger robustness than static or heuristic baselines.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.
